question: to the Commission Virginie Joron (PfE) Subject:

The Centre for Media Pluralism and Media Freedom is part of the Robert Schuman Centre at the European University Institute. It is co‑financed by the European Union, and has been monitoring levels of pluralism in European media since 2013–2014. Its 2026 report on France (Monitoring media pluralism in the European Union) states that ‘the French Government has supported initiatives such as Conspiracy Watch, headed by blogger Rudy Reichstadt and historian Valérie Igounet’. Founded in 2007, Conspiracy Watch has benefited from financial backing from the online media pluralism fund since 2018. However, its involvement in the Marianne Fund scandal – when an anti-extremism public fund was allegedly misused to favour associates of former minister Marlène Schiappa – has tarnished its reputation (Les Jours, 2023)s1. In view of the seriousness of these accusations: 1.
Has the Commission given Conspiracy Watch the opportunity to respond to these accusations?

Has it informed the European Digital Media Observatory, as well as any stakeholders interested in fact‑checking in relation to the Digital Services Act who are working with Conspiracy Watch2, of the negative assessment from the Robert Schuman Centre at the European University Institute?
Does the Commission publish the list of organisations that have unsuccessfully requested or lost the trusted flagger status under the Digital Services Act?

Alan Ouakrat and Raphaël Lupovici, ‘Monitoring media pluralism in the European Union: Results of the MPM2026, Country report: France’, https://cadmus.eui.eu/server/api/core/bitstreams/3e9a151d-65ae-48429d1b-d6e0d5a40087/content, p. 13. 2 https://moonshotteam.com/wp-content/uploads/Building-Resilience-to-Misinformation-in-Europe.pdf; https://belux.edmo.eu/fr/la-matrice-quelle-est-cette-thorie-du-complot-soutenue-par-andrew-tate/. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) The Centre for Media Pluralism (CMPF) is an independent research centre specialised in media freedom and pluralism, and the Media Pluralism Monitor (MPM) is a scientific tool analysing risks to media freedom across all Member States and selected enlargement countries. The Commission co-finances the project but in no way directs the CMPF or its country teams in the design and implementation of the MPM. The views expressed in the MPM publication reflect the opinion of individual authors, not of the Commission. The Commission takes the MPM findings into account to support its analysis of developments in the area of media freedom and pluralism in the annual rule of law report, in particular where they concern structural issues in a given Member State. The Commission does not take a position on the MPM reporting concerning specific cases or statements. The Commission has not reached out either to Conspiracy Watch, the European Digital Media Observatory, or any other stakeholders regarding the MPM findings quoted by the Honourable Member. Under Article 22 of the Digital Services Act1 (DSA), the trusted flagger status may be granted by the competent national Digital Services Coordinator to entities that demonstrate that they meet the eligibility conditions set out in Article 22(2). In accordance with Article 22(5) of the DSA, the Commission publishes information concerning entities that have been awarded trusted flagger status in a publicly available database2. The DSA does not establish an obligation to publish the identity of entities whose applications for trusted flagger status, submitted to the Digital Services Coordinators in the Member State in which they are established, were unsuccessful.
